sections.rule: One correct option. One mark each. No negative marking.
Multiple correct options. +1 for each right option, −1 for each wrong one, and a question cannot score below zero.

paper.caselet: A workflow tool has 300 enthusiastic customers, mostly small technical teams who tolerate rough edges and configure it themselves. Growth has stalled. Interviews with larger non-technical buyers find they want references from firms like their own, a guaranteed uptime figure, and someone to set it up for them.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Market to the whole non-technical buyer population at once so the reference base builds as fast as possible
Keep improving the product for the existing 300, since they are the customers who actually understand it
Pick one narrow segment of those buyers and build the complete offer that segment needs, references included
Raise the price so the product reads as enterprise-grade, which is what the larger buyers are looking for

paper.caselet: A team writes: "A cloud-native, event-driven ingestion pipeline with pluggable transformation stages and horizontal autoscaling." It is used on the website homepage, in the sales deck, and in the engineering backlog.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible criticism?
options: The statement is too technical, and rewriting it in simpler words for all three uses would resolve it
There is nothing wrong: a single consistent description across all channels is what alignment means
It should be shortened, because a homepage cannot carry a sentence of that length effectively
One statement is doing two different jobs, and it is written for the team rather than the buyer

paper.caselet: A first outbound email opens with a feature comparison table against three named competitors and a customer testimonial, and closes by asking the recipient to book a demo. Open rates are healthy; replies are close to zero.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible diagnosis?
options: The message answers questions a buyer only asks later, and never establishes the problem it solves
The channel is wrong, since outbound email no longer produces replies from any buyer segment
The email is too long, and cutting it to three sentences would raise the reply rate
The competitor comparison is the error, because naming rivals gives them free attention

paper.caselet: A specification reads: "The system shall export a payroll file. The export shall complete within 30 seconds for 5,000 employees. The export shall be available to users with the finance role only."
paper.stem: How should these three statements be classified?
options: One functional requirement, one quality requirement, and one design decision that is not among the requirements
Three quality requirements, because none of them is functional and all constrain the finished system
Three functional requirements, since each describes something the system must do rather than a quality it must have
One functional requirement and two quality requirements constraining how well it must be done

paper.caselet: A commuter buys a coffee from the same stall every weekday at 07:40. Asked why, he says the queue is short so he is not late, the cup gives him something to hold on a crowded platform, and arriving at his desk with it makes him feel the day has started properly.
paper.stem: What is this purchase actually serving?
options: A habit formed by repetition, since the same purchase made at the same time each weekday has become automatic behaviour requiring no decision
A caffeine requirement, which is what any coffee purchase fundamentally comes down to in the end
Getting to work on time, having something to do while waiting, and starting the day feeling ready
Price sensitivity, because a stall is cheaper than the cafe and cost is what decides a daily purchase

paper.caselet: A tool cuts a mid-size insurer's claims-handling time by 12,000 staff-hours a year, worth about ₹2.4 crore. Building and running it costs the vendor ₹40 lakh a year. The vendor proposes a price of ₹52 lakh, reached by adding a 30% margin to cost.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible criticism of the pricing?
options: Nothing is wrong, since a price that covers cost and leaves a margin is a sustainable price
The 30% margin is too thin for software, and a higher percentage on the same base would fix it
The price is too high, because ₹52 lakh is more than the ₹40 lakh the product actually costs to deliver
The price is anchored to what the vendor spends rather than to the ₹2.4 crore the customer gains

paper.caselet: A release has capacity for six items. A regulator has mandated an audit log for the same date. Every one of the eleven candidate items has been marked Must have by the stakeholder who proposed it, and no item is marked Won't have.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible criticism of this prioritisation?
options: Marking everything Must have removes the method's only output, and refusing to name any Won't have is what allows it
The regulator's audit log should be ranked alongside the others, since a scoring method treats all items alike
The problem is that eleven items is too many to score, and the list should be cut before prioritising
Nothing is wrong, since the stakeholders are closest to their own items and know their true importance

paper.caselet: A fitness product plans to collect location traces continuously so that a route-suggestion feature can be built later. There is no route feature yet. Users are asked to accept a privacy policy at signup that mentions location among fourteen other categories, and the data will be processed by a vendor outside the company.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible criticism?
options: The plan is acceptable, since the user has accepted a policy that does mention location collection, and consent given at signup covers whatever is later built from the data
Location data should never be collected by a fitness product under any circumstances, since the category is sensitive enough that no purpose could justify holding it
The privacy policy needs to be shorter, so that users can reasonably read all fifteen categories before accepting, after which the collection described in it becomes properly consented
Data is being collected for a purpose that does not yet exist, under a consent that does not identify it, and passed to a vendor whose handling has not been established

paper.caselet: A student can state what Desirability, feasibility, viability is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Desirability, feasibility, viability to the wider subject?
options: A product survives only where customer value, engineering reality, and business economics overlap; one cannot compensate indefinitely for another.
Desirability, feasibility, viability improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Desirability, feasibility, viability works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Desirability, feasibility, viability has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.caselet: A new privacy requirement invalidates a planned data feature, but the roadmap still shows it as committed.
paper.stem: What is the responsible product response?
options: Hide the change from the stakeholders until after the release has already gone out to customers in production.
Trace the affected requirement, revise priorities and the roadmap, and communicate how the strategic outcome will be met safely.
Build it unchanged, because a published roadmap cannot be moved once it has been committed to publicly.
Delete the privacy requirement from the backlog entirely so that the original delivery date can still be held as promised.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Competition and alternatives?
options: Competition and alternatives: Competition includes every current or potential way customers accomplish the job, including substitutes and doing nothing—not only similar products.
Competition and alternatives: Only firms shipping the same feature list should be counted as competitors in this particular market.
Competition and alternatives: Competition should be defined first, before anyone works out the customer's underlying job.
Competition and alternatives: Customers cannot compare a product against manual work or against doing nothing about the problem.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Functional and quality requirements is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Functional and quality requirements to the wider subject?
options: Once Functional and quality requirements has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
A capability is incomplete without the quality conditions that make it safe, usable, and compliant in the real product.
Functional and quality requirements works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Functional and quality requirements improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: A new enterprise tool delights technical pioneers but mainstream buyers ask for uptime, integration, references, security, and support.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Crossing the chasm: Win a narrow beachhead with a complete, credible solution and use its references before expanding.
Crossing the chasm: Dismiss the reliability concerns as ordinary resistance to innovation coming from the more conservative buyers.
Crossing the chasm: Target the whole market at once, before proving that even one repeatable use case works reliably.
Crossing the chasm: Add more experimental features aimed at every possible segment at the same time.

paper.caselet: A regulated Indian investing app could theoretically help global investors but can currently serve Indian online retail users and initially targets cost-conscious self-directed investors.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: TAM, SAM, and SOM: Call all global investors SOM, because a digital product can technically reach any one of them anywhere in the world.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Ignore regulation entirely when defining SAM, since rules do not change who could theoretically buy.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Call the initial segment TAM, because that is the group which will be contacted first in the campaign.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Treat global investors as TAM, Indian online retail investors as SAM, and the reachable cost-conscious segment as SOM.

paper.caselet: A student can state what TAM, SAM, and SOM is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects TAM, SAM, and SOM to the wider subject?
options: Once TAM, SAM, and SOM has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Market sizing becomes actionable by narrowing theoretical need through service constraints to the customers the current product can actually win.
TAM, SAM, and SOM works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
TAM, SAM, and SOM improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Product definition and positioning?
options: Product definition and positioning: A positioning statement is really an internal technical specification, written for the engineering team to build the product from during the development phase itself.
Product definition and positioning: Product definition and positioning are identical feature lists, written out twice over for two different internal audiences to read and then approve before launch.
Product definition and positioning: Positioning does not require naming either a target user or the alternative the product is being compared against by the buyer at the time of purchase.
Product definition and positioning: Definition clarifies what is built and why; positioning always states the differentiated value to one target customer against alternatives.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Value-based pricing?
options: Value-based pricing: All customer segments receive the same value from the product and should therefore be charged an identical price for it.
Value-based pricing: Value-based pricing always starts from measurable customer value and willingness to pay, never from cost or the competitor's price.
Value-based pricing: Value can be priced without ever being articulated or measured, since the customer already knows what it is worth to them anyway.
Value-based pricing: Price should always equal unit cost plus a fixed markup, whatever the customer actually gains from using it.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains TAM, SAM, and SOM?
options: TAM, SAM, and SOM: TAM is the set of customers that the current sales team expects to win during this quarter from its existing pipeline of qualified leads and nothing more than that.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: TAM, SAM and SOM always narrow in that order: theoretical demand, the servable portion, then the realistic near-term share.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Regulation, channel, and capability do not affect the serviceable market, since anyone who has the need is theoretically reachable by the product at some point in time.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: SOM is always larger than SAM, because the obtainable market includes every single future market that the firm might eventually decide it wants to enter in future.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Value-based pricing is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Value-based pricing to the wider subject?
options: Once Value-based pricing has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Value-based pricing improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Pricing captures part of created value; clear segmentation and value evidence connect customer benefit to business viability.
Value-based pricing works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A team has a technically feasible product for a huge TAM but cannot name the customer progress it improves.
paper.stem: What should happen before scaling?
options: Set a price for the product before identifying what customer outcome it is actually meant to deliver for anyone who buys it.
Return to the customer job and desirability evidence, then narrow to a reachable segment whose unmet progress the product can serve.
Increase the TAM estimates until the business case finally works on the spreadsheet in front of you.
Add more features to the product, because demonstrated technical feasibility is itself proof of real customer value here.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Product roadmap?
options: Product roadmap: A roadmap is an unchangeable promise of exactly which features will ship, and on exactly which dates, for years into the future.
Product roadmap: A roadmap turns strategy into an adaptable sequence of outcomes, always carrying more detail near term than far term.
Product roadmap: It is identical to the current sprint backlog, written out in a different format for a different audience each quarter.
Product roadmap: Market and technology change should not affect the roadmap, because a plan that keeps moving is not a plan.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Requirements traceability?
options: Requirements traceability: Once a requirement is written down, its original source and its tests can safely be discarded from the record.
Requirements traceability: Traceability is only a list of developer tasks kept inside the team's project tracking tool.
Requirements traceability: Traceability links every customer need through requirement, implementation and verification, so scope and change stay explainable.
Requirements traceability: Customer requirements and project requirements should never be connected to one another anywhere in the documentation.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Functional and quality requirements?
options: Functional and quality requirements: Quality requirements do not need measurable conditions attached to them, since their general intent is already understood by everyone on the team.
Functional and quality requirements: Functional requirements state what the product must do and quality requirements how well; a capability is never complete without both.
Functional and quality requirements: A functional requirement describes only the colour and layout of the user interface as it finally appears on the screen.
Functional and quality requirements: Security and performance are always optional feature requests that can be added later on if there is time.

paper.caselet: A subscription spends ₹1,000 to acquire a customer and earns ₹100 monthly gross profit from that customer.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Unit economics: Ignore churn entirely, because the acquisition spend has already been committed, and a sunk cost cannot be recovered by studying how long the customer stays.
Unit economics: Compare CAC only with the top-line company revenue and stop the analysis there without looking at contribution.
Unit economics: Call the payback period one month, because the subscription happens to bill on a monthly cycle to the customer each time.
Unit economics: Recognise a ten-month CAC payback before considering retention, cash burn, and whether lifetime gross profit comfortably exceeds acquisition cost.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation?
options: MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: A numeric score eliminates the need to examine the assumptions that produced that number in the first place anyway.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: MoSCoW sorts necessity and RICE compares reach, impact, confidence and effort; neither ever replaces judgement.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Every stakeholder request should be marked a Must have so that nobody involved is left disappointed.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: RICE ignores effort and confidence entirely, and ranks competing ideas on reach and impact alone when scoring them.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Actionable product metrics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Actionable product metrics to the wider subject?
options: Actionable product metrics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
A metric earns its place when evidence can change resource allocation, product action, or risk response.
Once Actionable product metrics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Actionable product metrics works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: Software saves one segment ₹10 lakh a year but saves another only ₹50,000, while serving both costs roughly the same.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Value-based pricing: Ignore the measurable savings the customer gains, because software has a low marginal cost.
Value-based pricing: Charge both segments from an identical delivery cost, since the software is the same.
Value-based pricing: Use the different economic value and willingness to pay to shape segment-specific offers and price structure.
Value-based pricing: Set the price from the cheaper alternative's feature count alone.

paper.caselet: Potential users do not yet recognise a health-monitoring problem, but the campaign opens with a detailed comparison of advanced settings.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Buyer journey communication: Use the same decision-stage proof on audiences who are not yet aware that the problem exists at all.
Buyer journey communication: Add every technical specification into the very first message the buyer receives, on the view that more information always moves a decision forward.
Buyer journey communication: First make the problem and relevant value understandable, then introduce alternatives and proof as the buyer advances.
Buyer journey communication: Wait until after the purchase is complete before explaining any of the value to the customer.

paper.caselet: Two features differ in user reach, likely impact, evidence confidence, and engineering effort, while a legal capability is non-negotiable.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Put all three items into the Must have category so that no conflict arises between the stakeholders.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Choose the idea with the highest claimed impact and ignore the confidence and effort scores entirely when ranking them.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Mark the legal capability as Must and use a transparent RICE comparison for discretionary features, then review assumptions.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Let the loudest stakeholder in the room set the order of the whole backlog each time, since their conviction is the clearest signal of what matters.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Requirements traceability is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Requirements traceability to the wider subject?
options: Requirements traceability works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Traceability preserves the reason behind work, making change impact and completion evidence visible across the development chain.
Requirements traceability improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Requirements traceability has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.

paper.caselet: Customers report high value and accept the price, but acquisition payback is longer than typical retention.
paper.stem: What does the evidence imply?
options: Increase acquisition spending further, because every additional signup adds revenue straight to the top line each month it renews.
Ignore retention entirely when calculating lifetime value, since that customer has already been won and counted.
The offer may create value, but its acquisition or retention economics must change before growth is sustainable.
High willingness to pay proves the whole business model is viable on its own.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Unit economics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Unit economics to the wider subject?
options: Growth consumes cash before contribution repays acquisition; per-unit economics shows whether scaling improves or deepens the problem.
Once Unit economics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Unit economics works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Unit economics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.caselet: A student can state what MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation to the wider subject?
options: Prioritisation turns scarce capacity into an explicit decision by separating necessity from comparative value and evidence.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Privacy by design is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Privacy by design to the wider subject?
options: Once Privacy by design has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Privacy by design improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Data value does not remove accountability; product architecture determines whether privacy obligations can actually be honoured.
Privacy by design works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Crossing the chasm is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Crossing the chasm to the wider subject?
options: Crossing the chasm works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Crossing the chasm improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Crossing the chasm has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Early enthusiasm proves possibility; mainstream adoption depends on reducing the practical and social risk of switching.

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of a product roadmap.
options: It sequences development, release and evolution against a time axis
It follows from a product strategy, which it turns into releases
It is the inventory of every capability the product will eventually contain
Once published it should be held fixed, since changing it undermines the commitments made from it
What has been deliberately left out is part of the decision it records

paper.caselet: A subscription business earns ₹1,800 of gross profit per customer per year. It spends ₹5,400 to acquire one. Customers stay an average of four years. The finance lead reports that the business is profitable per customer and proposes raising acquisition spend.
paper.stem: Select every statement this case supports.
options: Because lifetime value exceeds acquisition cost, raising spend carries no additional risk
Acquisition cost is recovered in the third year of the relationship
Profitability per customer is established as soon as the first year's gross profit is earned
A payback measured in years is a cash-flow risk the profitability statement does not show
Lifetime gross profit of about ₹7,200 exceeds the ₹5,400 acquisition cost

paper.caselet: A hospital group tells a software vendor: "Our nurses waste time at shift handover and patients are at risk when something is missed." The vendor's product team decides the product will carry a structured handover record. The delivery team breaks that into a template editor for one release and an audit trail for the next.
paper.stem: Select every statement that classifies this chain correctly.
options: The hospital's statement is a project requirement, since it came from the party paying for the work
The hospital's statement is a customer requirement: a business need, not a specification
The structured handover record is the product requirement
The template editor and the audit trail are project requirements for particular releases
Standardising means building exactly what this hospital described, for this hospital

paper.caselet: A company sells compliance software to licensed pharmacies. There are 900,000 licensed pharmacies worldwide. Its product is certified only under Indian regulation, which covers 90,000 of them. Of those, 62,000 already run a competing system on multi-year contracts, and the firm's sales capacity can reach about 4,000 pharmacies in the coming year.
paper.stem: Select every statement that sizes this market correctly.
options: Regulatory certification is what narrows the total to a serviceable 90,000
The 62,000 on competing contracts should be counted in the serviceable market as switchable demand
The obtainable figure should be the 90,000 serviceable pharmacies, since sales capacity can be hired
About 4,000 is the obtainable share, because reach and competition bound it
The 900,000 figure is the total addressable market

paper.caselet: A team building an expense-reporting tool lists two rival products in its competitive review. Interviews find that of forty finance teams, twenty-six use a spreadsheet template, nine ask an assistant to compile receipts by hand, and five have decided the problem is not worth solving and simply absorb the errors.
paper.stem: The review already lists the two rival products. Select every further alternative this case shows the product is really competing against.
options: The other finance software these teams already pay for that does not touch expenses
The spreadsheet template twenty-six teams currently rely on
The two rival products, which should be counted again as the primary competition
The decision by five teams to do nothing about the problem
The manual compilation nine teams pay an assistant to do

paper.caselet: A logistics startup has built a route-planning tool. Drivers who trialled it completed their rounds sooner and asked to keep it. The engineering team ships updates weekly on existing map infrastructure. The company charges ₹400 per driver per month; the support and mapping licence cost per driver is ₹430, and neither falls with volume.
paper.stem: Select every statement this case supports.
options: The idea fails on viability, because each additional driver deepens the loss
The idea is proven overall, since two of the three checks are clearly passed
Viability can be assumed from the drivers' enthusiasm, because demand sets price
Feasibility holds: it is being built and shipped with technology that exists now
Desirability holds: the people who used it wanted to carry on using it

paper.caselet: A six-month-old product reports to its board each month on registered accounts, page views, and press mentions. All three rise steadily. Weekly active use has been flat since month two, and no one has been asked to act on any of the three reported numbers.
paper.stem: Select every criticism this reporting fairly attracts.
options: The measure that would show whether the product is working is the one not being reported
The reporting is appropriate, since a board is entitled to see growth figures at this stage
No number carries an owner or a threshold, so none of them can require a decision
Registered accounts is the right headline measure, because it is the figure that has grown most
The reported measures rise whatever happens, so they cannot separate progress from activity

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of what a Lean Canvas is for.
options: It replaces the Business Model Canvas boxes that suit an established company with ones a startup needs
A box left empty is a failure of the exercise and should be filled before the canvas is used
Its value is that a wrong box is cheap to discover and cheap to change
It is a document to be completed once and then held stable for the investor conversation
It records the assumptions a business rests on so they can be tested

paper.stem: Select every strategy that helps a product cross from its early market to the mainstream.
options: Raise the price at launch so mainstream buyers read it as quality
Focus on a narrow beachhead market rather than spray and pray
Address the early market and the mainstream at the same time to build volume faster
Build trust through uptime, security, support, compliance, and social proof
Simplify onboarding and the interface for mainstream users

paper.stem: Select every metric correctly paired with what it measures.
options: Average revenue per user — revenue divided across the user base
Gross margin — profitability measured after all below-the-line costs
Customer lifetime value — what a customer is worth across the whole relationship, not one transaction
Net promoter score — the startup-appropriate replacement for reducing uncertainty

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of cost-based pricing.
options: It is the fallback for when you do not know how the product will be deployed, or what it does to the customer's business
It prices your own inputs rather than the customer's outcome
It is the method to prefer once the product has a measurable economic value peg
Billing by engineer hours at $50 or $200 an hour is the familiar software-services case
It is what the lecture recommends for software products in particular

paper.stem: Select every box that appears on the Lean Canvas but not on the Business Model Canvas.
options: Channels
Customer segments
Problem
Unfair advantage
Solution

paper.caselet:
WhatsApp started in 2009, into a market that already had Skype, Yahoo Messenger, ICQ and plenty more.

It launched on iPhone. Android followed around the middle of 2011 — and the team already knew that a large share of the people it wanted were on Android, in Asia.

The rest arrived on its own schedule: message history search around 2011, chat backup after 2012. The company was acquired in 2014 still without end-to-end encryption.
paper.stem: Select every statement that reads this release history the way the course does.
options: A roadmap is a smart sequence for developing, releasing, and evolving a solution
Launching on iPhone first shows the team did not know where its users were
The Android delay was a resourcing accident rather than a decision
A roadmap is a set of releases with no strategic horizon behind it
The team launched on iPhone knowing a big chunk of its potential users were on Android in Asia

paper.stem: A customer says the product must send a message, and must deliver it within 200 milliseconds. Select every statement that classifies this correctly.
options: Sending the message is a functional requirement — an action the product performs
The 200-millisecond bound is functional, because it describes what the product does
Both halves are non-functional, because the customer stated them in one sentence
The 200-millisecond bound is non-functional — a quality, confirmed by measurement under load

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of testing an idea for desirability, feasibility and viability.
options: Viability is settled once a working prototype exists
Desirability is validated with design skills and empathy for the customer
Feasibility asks whether the product can be built with the technology available today
A product that is desirable and feasible but not viable is unsustainable
Feasibility is confirmed by customer interviews showing people want the product

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of how MoSCoW is used.
options: Won't have is part of the method, and stating it is what makes scope control real
It works as a filtering criterion, closer to a triage than to a ranking
It ranks every item against every other to produce one ordered list
Moscow refers to the capital city, where the technique was first formalised

paper.stem: Select every statement that is correct about these data-protection regimes.
options: GDPR was enacted in May 2018 and became a model for Switzerland, Canada, and Australia
GDPR protects any personal data irrespective of its sensitivity
Data protection by design means the customer must request that their data be protected
US data protection is a single federal regime covering every category of data alike
US data protection leaves employee data outside its data protection regulations

paper.stem: Select every statement that correctly traces a customer need into a project requirement.
options: Project requirements are written by the customer and passed to engineering unchanged
Customer requirements arrive already standardised, because customers state system requirements
Customer requirements describe business needs and aspirations rather than system specifications
Project requirements break a product requirement down for a release across smaller teams
Standardising generalises one customer's stated need so more customers of that nature are served by one product

paper.stem: Select every business type correctly paired with the unit its economics should be measured on.
options: The unit is whichever one makes the economics look strongest to investors
Marketplace — one customer lifetime
SaaS — one customer or account
E-commerce — one order
Ride-sharing — one ride

paper.stem: Select every statement that is true of a product roadmap.
options: It fixes the next three to six months and deliberately goes no further
What has been deliberately deferred is as much a part of it as what has been scheduled
It translates product strategy into a series of releases on a time axis
It lists the features to build without ordering them, leaving sequence to the team
